lessons.title: Rent Changes, City Moves and Job Switches During the Year

body.text: Real years are messy. Rent goes up at renewal, companies transfer people, people switch jobs. The rule is simple: split the year every time salary, HRA, rent or city changes, apply the three limits to each piece, then add up. Doing it on annual totals can overstate your claim.

children.text: Lessons 4 to 7 assumed nothing changed from April to March. For many salaried Indians that is rarely true. An 11-month rent agreement renews with a 5% to 10% hike, an appraisal in July lifts basic pay, a transfer moves you from Lucknow to Bengaluru, or a new offer takes you from Chennai to Mumbai. This lesson shows how to handle each of those correctly.

markDefs.definition: The period in the tax year during which you occupied the rented accommodation. When figures change within that period, the calculation is done separately for each stretch of months with the same figures.

children.text: Rule 279 of the Income-tax Rules, 2026 measures HRA, rent and salary for the

, the time you occupied the rented home. The widely followed practice, used by employers and tax officers, is to work out the three limits separately for every stretch of months in which the figures stay the same, and add the results.

body.label: Where to split the year
body.value: Any change in salary, HRA, rent or city
body.context: Also split for months with no HRA (such as a gap between jobs) or no rent (such as living with family). Those months contribute nothing to the exemption.

body.caption: Each period i uses its own HRA, rent, salary and city percentage. A negative Limit 2 counts as zero for that period.

children.text: Ananya works in Pune on a basic salary of ₹70,000 and HRA of ₹35,000 a month. She paid ₹28,000 a month in Baner from April to October. Her agreement renewed in November at ₹31,000.
Her total exemption is ₹1,47,000 + ₹1,20,000 = ₹2,67,000. If she had simply added up the year, ₹3,51,000 of rent minus ₹84,000, she would get the same answer.

body.text: Annual totals give the right answer only when the same limit binds in every period and Limit 2 is positive throughout, as with Ananya. The moment the binding limit switches, or rent in one period is below 10% of salary, annual totals go wrong. The next two cases show both errors.

children.text: Case 2: The Transfer to a New City

Rohan works for a bank and is transferred from Lucknow to Bengaluru on 1 October. His basic salary stays at ₹80,000 a month. His HRA rises from 40% of basic (₹32,000) to 50% of basic (₹40,000). In Lucknow he paid ₹18,000 a month for a flat in Gomti Nagar. In Bengaluru he pays ₹60,000 in Indiranagar.

body.title: Rohan's exemption: two ways to calculate

columns.label: Annual totals (wrong)
points: Claimed exemption: ₹3,72,000, which is ₹72,000 too high
Also forces a single city percentage on a year spent in two cities

body.title: Why annual totals overstate Rohan's claim

children.text: In Bengaluru, Rohan's high rent pushes Limit 2 to ₹3,12,000, but he can only exempt ₹2,40,000 because that is all the HRA he received there. The unused ₹72,000 of Limit 2 is simply lost. When you pool the year, that unused Bengaluru rent quietly spills over and "covers" the Lucknow months, where his low rent kept Limit 2 at just ₹60,000. The law does not allow rent in one home to support HRA for a period when you lived somewhere else, so the period method is the one to follow.
Meera left an IT services company in Chennai on 30 June and joined a fintech in Mumbai on 1 July. She moved flats with the job.

events.title: Employer A, Chennai
events.description: Basic ₹60,000, HRA ₹24,000 a month. Rent ₹25,000 a month in Adyar. Employer A deducts TDS under Section 392 and gives her the HRA exemption for these three months.

events.title: Joins Employer B, Mumbai
events.description: Submits Form 122 with her salary and TDS from Employer A, and Form 124 with her new rent details and landlord PAN.

events.title: Employer B, Mumbai
events.description: Basic ₹90,000, HRA ₹45,000 a month. Rent ₹55,000 a month in Powai.

events.title: Two salary TDS certificates

headers: Employer A, Chennai: April to June
Employer B, Mumbai: July to March

body.text: When you switch jobs, your new employer does not know what your previous employer paid or exempted unless you tell them in Form 122 (which replaced Form 12B). Skip it and both employers may apply lower slab rates, leaving you with a large tax bill at filing time. Also check that each Form 130 shows HRA exemption only for the months you worked there, so the exemption is not counted twice.

body.title: Quick Check: Two Rents in One Month
body.question: In July, Meera paid ₹25,000 for her Chennai flat because of her notice period with the landlord, and ₹55,000 for her new Mumbai flat, where she was already living. Which rent counts for July?
options: Only the Chennai rent, because that agreement came first
Only the Mumbai rent, because that is the home she occupied
Neither, because she paid two rents
body.explanation: The exemption is for rent on the accommodation you occupy. In July, Meera lived in Mumbai, so only the ₹55,000 counts. The Chennai payment is a real cost, but it is not rent for a home she occupied in that month.

body.title: Quick Check: The Gap Between Jobs
body.question: Varun resigns from a Hyderabad company on 31 August and joins a new company on 1 November. He keeps paying ₹22,000 a month rent for his Madhapur flat throughout. What is his HRA exemption for September and October?
options: Calculated using his old HRA and salary
Nil, because he received no HRA in those months
body.explanation: Limit 1 is the HRA actually received. With no salary and no HRA for September and October, Limit 1 is zero for that period, so the exemption is zero. Rent paid while between jobs does not create an exemption, and it cannot be carried to another period.

body.title: Try It: Kiran's Mid-Year Upgrade
body.prompt: Kiran works in Hyderabad with a basic salary of ₹50,000 and HRA of ₹25,000 a month all year. He paid ₹20,000 a month rent from April to September, then moved to a bigger flat at ₹32,000 a month from October to March. Using the period method, what is his total exempt HRA for tax year 2026-27? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: April to September: salary ₹3,00,000, HRA ₹1,50,000, Limit 2 is ₹1,20,000 minus ₹30,000 = ₹90,000, Limit 3 ₹1,50,000. Exempt: ₹90,000. October to March: HRA ₹1,50,000, Limit 2 is ₹1,92,000 minus ₹30,000 = ₹1,62,000, Limit 3 ₹1,50,000. Exempt: ₹1,50,000. Total ₹2,40,000. Annual totals would give ₹2,52,000, overstating by ₹12,000, because the binding limit switched from Limit 2 to Limits 1 and 3.

body.title: Scenario: Moving Into His Own Flat
body.scenario: Sahil rents in Prahlad Nagar, Ahmedabad, at ₹30,000 a month. His basic salary is ₹75,000 and HRA ₹37,500 a month. He takes possession of a flat he bought in Bopal and moves in on 1 January 2027. His rent agreement has a lock-in, so he pays rent for the old flat for January and February too, though it stands empty. He is on the old regime.
body.prompt: Which months count for his HRA exemption, what is the exempt amount, and what should he tell his employer?
body.modelAnswer: Only April to December 2026, nine months, count. From 1 January he lives in a home he owns, so Tests 3 and 4 from Lesson 2 fail, and the January and February rent is for a flat he no longer occupies. For the nine months: salary ₹6,75,000, HRA ₹3,37,500, rent ₹2,70,000. Limit 2 is ₹2,70,000 minus ₹67,500 = ₹2,02,500; Limit 3 is ₹3,37,500. Exempt HRA is ₹2,02,500. His HRA for January to March, ₹1,12,500, is fully taxable. He should update his declaration with his employer as soon as he moves, so TDS for January to March is correct and he does not face a shortfall at filing. If he took a home loan, the interest may now qualify for a separate benefit, covered in Lesson 10.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: Telling Your New Employer
body.textWithBlank: When you join a new employer mid-year, you report your previous employer's salary and TDS in Form ___, which replaced Form 12B.
body.explanation: Form 122 under the Income-tax Rules, 2026 lets your new employer include your earlier salary when calculating TDS under Section 392 for the rest of the year. Your rent and HRA claims go separately in Form 124.

body.title: Map Your Own Year
steps: List every month from April to March in a column
Next to each month, note your basic, DA, HRA, rent and the city of the home you lived in
Draw a line wherever any of those figures changes, and mark months with no HRA or no rent
Calculate the three limits separately for each block of unchanged months
Add the exempt amounts, then compare with the total shown across your Form 130 certificates
If you changed jobs, confirm you gave Form 122 to your new employer and that no month is counted by both employers

cards.definition: Splitting the tax year wherever salary, HRA, rent or city changes, applying the three limits to each period and adding the results.
Using annual totals when figures changed during the year. It overstates the exemption when the binding limit switches, and misstates it when rent in one period was below 10% of salary.
The form under the Income-tax Rules, 2026 for giving a new employer details of salary and TDS from a previous employer in the same tax year. Replaced Form 12B.
The certificate of TDS on salary under Section 395 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. Replaced Form 16. Each employer issues one.
Only rent for the home you actually live in counts. Rent for an empty flat during a notice period or lock-in does not.

points: Split the year wherever salary, HRA, rent or city changes, calculate the three limits for each period and add them up
Annual totals only work when the same limit binds throughout. Otherwise they can overstate your exemption
After a transfer, each city uses its own percentage and its own rent. Rent in one city cannot support HRA for months spent in another
Months with no HRA, such as a gap between jobs, give no exemption even if you pay rent
Only rent for the home you occupy counts. Rent on a vacated flat during a lock-in or notice period does not
On a job switch, give your new employer Form 122 and your rent details in Form 124, and check each Form 130 before you file
